newsitem.title: USA: Greenspan repeats concern over market levels.
newsitem.headline: Greenspan repeats concern over market levels.

text.p: U.S. Federal Reserve Board Chairman Alan Greenspan urged caution about the huge increase in the stock market, again issuing his warning about "irrational exuberance" of investors.

In prepared testimony before the Senate Banking Committee, Greenspan noted that last December he wondered out loud about when such exuberance leads to escalated asset values, which can become subject to unexpected and prolonged protractions.
"We have not been able, as yet, to provide a satisfying answer to this question, but there are reasons in the current environment to keep this question on the table," he said.

"As you know, last December, I put the question this way: ... how do we know when irrational exuberance has unduly escalated asset values, which then become subject to unexpected and prolonged contractions?" he said.
Since issuing that remark, which temporarily stunned financial markets, the U.S. stock market has recovered and is now higher than when he first raised a cautionary flag.
Greenspan also took aim at the considerable optimism that has led to "quality spreads on high-yield corporate bonds -- what we used to call junk bonds."

"Considerable optimism about the ability of businesses to sustain this current healthy financial condition seems ... to be influencing the setting of risk premiums, not just the stock market, but throughout the financial system," he said.
"It is not that we have a firm view that equity prices are necessarily excessive right now, or risk spreads patently too low," he said.

He argued that the goal of the Fed was to contribute to the highest-possible income growth and wealth over time and would "be pleased if the favorable economic environment projected in markets actually comes to pass."
But he cautioned that the interest-rate setting Federal Open Market Committee has to be sensitive to indications of "even slowly building imbalances, whatever their source."
At the same time, Greenspan expressed some surprise that the "more than $4 trillion rise in equity values since late 1994" had not had a larger impact on consumer spending.
"It is possible, however, that households have been reluctant to spend much of their added wealth because they see a greater need to keep it to support spending in retirement," he said.
